query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.intervention: optimizing the lamellar colony size and internal boundary structure through advanced processing techniques
generation.material_initial_state: dual-phase lamellar colonies in eutectic high-entropy alloys
generation.mechanism: reducing microcracking initiation and propagation by increasing the internal boundary area and modifying the colony size
generation.predicted_outcome: improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility
generation.boundary: processing techniques that can control lamellar colony size and internal boundary structure
generation.uncertainty: the optimal colony size and internal boundary structure for maximizing strength and ductility
generation.falsification_experiment: tensile deformation tests on samples with optimized and unoptimized lamellar colony structures
generation.structural_mediator: internal boundaries within the lamellar colonies
generation.hypothesis: optimizing the lamellar colony size and internal boundary structure can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys
